item.title: Reasoning at Constant Memory: How a 4B Chinese Open Model Freezes the KV Cache at 72 MiB
item.guid: title:reasoning at constant memory how a 4b chinese open model freezes the kv cache at 72 mib
item.description: Inside EdgeRock-4B’s “Rock Memory Anchors” — and what they mean for anyone serving long-reasoning models Every engineer who has served a reasoning model knows the moment. The model is good, the answers are right, and then someone sends a 64K-token agent trace and the GPU's memory graph turns into a staircase. Reasoning models think out loud, and every token they think costs KV cache. On October 19, 2026, a team from Rock Matrix (岩芯矩阵, a unit of Chinese listed company 岩山科技), working with researchers at HKUST and CMU, open-sourced a model that takes a different route. EdgeRock-4B keeps its attention KV cache fixed at 72 MiB per sequence , whether the context is 4K tokens or 256K. At 256K that is 99.

item.title: Every Clock Says 10:10? How AI Actually Generates Images — Diffusion, Latent Space & Flow Matching
item.guid: title:every clock says 10 10 how ai actually generates images diffusion latent space flow matching
item.description: Every Clock Says 10:10? How AI Actually Generates Images — Diffusion, Latent Space & Flow Matching (Every Number Measured) Why every AI clock snaps to 10:10, how a 32-channel VAE cuts attention 65,536×, Tweedie’s formula, Classifier-Free Guidance, and 4-step Rectified Flow measured on a 96 GB Blackwell GPU. By Latent AI Labs (@LatentAILabs) In Part 1 ( YouTube ), we saw how an LLM turns words into vectors and why it miscounts the "r"s in "strawberry". In Part 2 ( YouTube ), we measured how thinking models catch their own mistakes by writing a scratchpad. And in Part 3 ( YouTube ), we opened all 1,152 attention heads across a 32,768-token book and found that just 16 Retrieval Heads (1. 4% of the model) copy-paste the facts.

item.title: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence
item.guid: title:kimi k3 open frontier intelligence
item.description: Today, we are introducing Kimi K3 — our most capable model. Kimi K3 is a 2. 8T-parameter model built on our Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals, with native vision capabilities and a 1-million-token context window. It is the world's first open 3T-class model, designed for frontier intelligence across long-horizon coding, knowledge work, and reasoning. While its overall performance still trails the most powerful proprietary models, Claude Fable 5 and GPT 5. 6 Sol, Kimi K3 demonstrated frontier-level performance across our evaluation suite, consistently outperforming other tested models.

item.title: From Chatbot to AI Agent: Building a Voice Nutrition Companion with Rasa Mantle
item.guid: title:from chatbot to ai agent building a voice nutrition companion with rasa mantle
item.description: Notes from building a voice-first nutrition companion with Rasa Mantle: how a chatbot becomes an agent, and what skills, deterministic tools and memory look like in practice. TL;DR The story: I built NourishHer, a voice-first nutrition companion on Rasa Mantle, through the Rasa Heroes program to find out how an agent differs from a chatbot. What I built: 16 skills and 15 deterministic tools. The core idea: the model understands, routes and phrases. Code owns saving data, nutrient numbers and safety wording. Mantle gives you building blocks to enforce that: skill gating ( requires: ), tool constraints, ordered steps and fixed replies.

item.title: Introducing PerceptionBench
item.guid: title:introducing perceptionbench
item.description: Evaluating Atomic Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models Authors Kimi Team We are releasing PerceptionBench , a benchmark that isolates visual perception and evaluates it as a set of atomic capabilities— discovered from how today's models fail, not defined in advance. From frontier-model failures across 42 benchmarks, we derive 10 atomic perceptual capabilities and construct 3,000 verified questions, each isolating a single capability and answerable by looking, with no reasoning or external knowledge required.

item.title: The Interpretability team studies how large language models work internally as a foundation for AI safety. They seek to understand what happens inside neural networks so that we can better trust the models we build.
item.guid: title:the interpretability team studies how large language models work internally as a foundation for ai safety they seek to understand what happens inside neural networks so that we can better trust the models we build
item.description: It’s hard to reason about the safety of neural networks without understanding what happens inside them. Our goal is to be able to explain large language models’ behavior, and to use that understanding to identify problems that are hard to see from the outside, such as situations where a model’s stated reasoning differs from what it’s actually doing. Our early work focused on mapping the internal mechanisms of AI models. Today, we increasingly apply our methods to real models to understand how they think and why they behave the way they do. We’ve developed techniques that allow us to understand models’ inner workings in plain language, making it easier to detect unsafe behavior or dishonest reasoning and safeguard against it. item.title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
item.guid: title:monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
item.description: There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal . I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts. First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability: Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval).

item.title: I Replaced Claude Code’s /compact With Dijkstra
item.guid: title:i replaced claude code s compact with dijkstra
item.description: A session graph, shortest paths and a knapsack kept every rule at half the tokens of a summary. Then the next task cost twice as much. I looked at the compactions in my own long Claude Code sessions. Each /compact read between 437k and 830k tokens, took 134 to 182 seconds, and produced a summary of 20k to 28k characters. That summary is everything the rest of the session knows about what came before. A model wrote it in one pass, deciding on its own what would matter later.

item.title: How Zip's AI Superagents Automate Procurement End-to-End | Rujul Zaparde
item.guid: title:how zip s ai superagents automate procurement end to end rujul zaparde
item.description: Every business in the world has to procure things, and for most of them, that process is slow, manual, and full of money left on the table. Rujul Zaparde, co-founder of Zip, joins Craig to explain how his company is using AI Superagents to change that: from autonomously redlining contracts and running supplier RFPs, to pushing approved data directly into enterprise systems like SAP and Oracle. With over $1. 2 trillion in cumulative spend processed - and Anthropic and OpenAI as customers - Zip isn't just experimenting with AI. It's building the governance infrastructure that makes agentic AI safe to deploy where the stakes are highest. The conversation goes well beyond procurement software.

item.title: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
item.guid: title:single tenant titus vm level isolation on a multi tenant container platform
item.description: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host.
